A's integration test queries prisma directly so it still passes, and B's cache tests don't delete articles, so existing tests don't catch it. B's invalidation assumption (tags only change on create) is broken by A.

rows.explanation: Change A makes userUpdatePrisma hash any password passed to it. Change B's new userChangePassword controller already hashes the new password with hashPassword before calling userUpdatePrisma. Merged, the new endpoint double-hashes: userUpdatePrisma hashes the already-hashed value, so the stored password is hash(hash(newPassword)). Subsequently logging in with newPassword compares against the double hash and fails, so a user who changes their password via POST /api/user/password is locked out of login with the new password. B's own test only checks the stored value is not plaintext and differs from before, so it still passes, as does A's test via PUT /api/user.

Change B adds a views counter that is incremented via prisma.article.update on every GET of an article. Combined, every article read now triggers an update that automatically sets updatedAt to now, so updatedAt no longer means 'last edited' and changes on every view. Before A, B's view increment would not touch updatedAt; after A, it does. This is a concrete runtime misbehavior arising only from the combination: article responses (and any ordering/display by updatedAt) will show the last-read time rather than the last-modified time.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A caches the tag list and invalidates it via a Prisma middleware on writes to Tag or Article models. Change B adds `prisma.tag.deleteMany(...)` after an article delete to remove orphan tags. Because the middleware matches `params.model === "Tag"` with action `deleteMany`, B's cleanup call triggers cache invalidation. Also, the article delete itself (model Article, action delete) already invalidates the cache, and the cleanup runs after it with its own invalidation. Both sequential operations await before the response, so the next GET /api/tags sees fresh data. There's a theoretical race where a concurrent GET between the article delete and tag cleanup repopulates the cache with the orphan tag, but the subsequent deleteMany invalidates the cache again, so staleness doesn't persist. Both changes are consistent in intent (cache vs. cleanup) and work correctly together.

At runtime they are fine together. In intent, though, both changes address the same problem, namely that passwords must be stored hashed when changed, using different mechanisms. B's changePassword test explicitly guards against plain-text storage, and A's new test covers the same property through PUT. The merged code has two independent password-changing paths with duplicated hashing responsibilities (hashing in the DB helper for one, in the controller for the other), so one hashing site should be consolidated. Weighing that the endpoints are distinct features (B adds current-password verification), the overlap is moderate but real.

Change B adds an ?after=<slug> cursor that filters with updatedAt < cursor.updatedAt while the query still orders by updatedAt (in B's own tree). After merging, the query orders by createdAt desc but the cursor filter still compares on updatedAt. The cursor therefore no longer matches the sort key. Concrete scenario: articles X (created Jan 1, edited Jan 10), Y (created Jan 2, updated Jan 2), Z (created Jan 3, updated Jan 3). The list order is Z, Y, X. Requesting ?after=Y filters updatedAt < Jan 2, which excludes X (updatedAt Jan 10) and returns nothing, even though X comes after Y in the list; ?after=X returns Y and Z, which come before X. Pagination via the cursor skips or repeats articles whenever updatedAt differs from createdAt order. B's test passes only because updatedAt and creation order coincide in it.
